research.fitAssessment: The name does not fit the product well. The job to be done is preparing for a specific conversation with a specific person: capture ideas over days, attach them to that person and the upcoming talk, let AI expand them into options, questions, objections and 'if they say X, ask Y' branches, then give a glanceable brief when the conversation happens and record the outcome afterward. 'Random Thought Organizer' says none of that. (1) It stresses the input ('random thoughts') instead of the payoff ('walk in prepared, forget nothing'). (2) It puts the product in the crowded generic brain-dump and thought-organizer category: Random Thoughts Journal, Mindscope - Thought Organizer, Journ - Thought Organizer, Quick Notes: Thought Organizer, a 'Thoughts Organizer' Chrome extension, and about 1.8k GitHub repos. The real differentiators, which are person and conversation scoping, branching contingencies and the at-the-moment brief, stay invisible. (3) 'Random' suggests unfocused. 'Organizer' is generic, and the US/UK split between 'Organizer' and 'Organiser' divides search. The user's own typo 'Organzier' also shows the name is easy to misspell. (4) The acronym has several strong collisions. RTO means Return to Office in current workplace language, which is especially bad for a tool often used to prep manager conversations that may be about RTO. It means Recovery Time Objective to the developer and IT audience that will first meet a Claude skill or plugin. And it means India's Regional Transport Office across both app stores, where 'RTO' searches are full of vehicle-info apps. A short handle like 'RTO' is convenient as a Claude slash command or internal codename, but it is hard to discover, easy to confuse, and hard to protect as a trademark. The concept space is real and thinly served: mathaka, Talk Topics, Talkfolio, Difficult Conversation Planner and Fellow's 1:1 agendas each cover part of it, and none combines personal and work conversations, capture over time, branching prep and a conversation-time brief. A name should claim that gap. Limitations of this check: US App Store searches only; Google Play results came from the Canada storefront; Justia and Trademarkia were blocked (403 / Cloudflare challenge) and tmsearch.uspto.gov was not queried directly, so the trademark findings rely on individual USPTO TSDR records and are not a clearance search.

research.recommendation:
Keep 'RTO' / 'random-thought-organizer' only as an internal codename. Rename before anything user-facing: a plugin or marketplace listing, a store app, a landing page or an MCP connector name.

Why:
(a) The acronym is already taken in every channel that matters. It means Return to Office in workplace language, Recovery Time Objective to the developer and IT audience that first meets a Claude plugin, and India's Regional Transport Office across both app stores, where 'RTO' searches are full of vehicle apps.
(b) The full name describes a generic brain-dump app in a crowded field and hides the real differentiator: preparing for a specific person and conversation, with branches and a brief at talk time.
(c) 'Random Thoughts' and 'Thought Organizer' are descriptive, crowded terms that would be hard to protect.
The codename is harmless for a solo private build: the repo folder, internal package IDs, and a personal /rto slash command where the context is unambiguous. Renaming is nearly free today and gets expensive after a store listing, a domain and users.

Preferred public name: TalkAhead. It had the lowest conflict of anything I checked. The only US mark I found (class 35 advertising) was cancelled in 2016, no app uses the name on the US App Store, and talkahead.app was available on 2026-09-25. It is brandable and works for both personal and work conversations.
Runner-up: 'Before We Talk'. It is the most self-explanatory and a natural skill trigger phrase, but a weak trademark; the old freelancer product's domain now redirects to an expired-domains listing, and beforewetalk.app was available.
Avoid: Hold That Thought, PrepTalk, Talking Points, Talk Tree, Parley, Pocket Brief, TalkBrief (all high conflict), and 'Loose Threads' (live apparel mark, quilting-dominated search).
Tagline to pair with the name: 'Ready to Talk'.

Before a public launch:
- Run a proper USPTO search (tmsearch.uspto.gov) for the chosen name in classes 9, 42 and 35, plus a common-law web and app-store sweep. I could not query tmsearch, and Justia and Trademarkia were blocked, so this review is not a clearance opinion.
- Consider a low-cost attorney knockout search if the product will be sold.
- Register the .app and .com domains yourself if they are still free (I did not buy anything).

Product signal from this research: the niche is real but thinly served. mathaka covers per-person memory briefs, Talk Topics covers per-person topic lists and was last updated in 2022, Talkfolio (Japan) covers small-talk topics per person, and Difficult Conversation Planner has 10+ downloads. Fellow is the strong incumbent for work 1:1s and already exposes agenda and talking-point generation to Claude through its MCP server. Position against Fellow on personal conversations (spouse, contractor, friend) plus work, capture over time from voice (Pocket), and branching 'if they say X, ask Y' prep.

omissions: The research calls 'RTO' hard to protect but never checked for existing marks, and there are live USPTO registrations for RTO itself. Rohde & Schwarz holds RTO in class 9 (oscilloscopes, reg. 5121647, live, Section 71 accepted May 2026). 360training.com (Ready Training) holds RTO in classes 9 and 41 (serial 87281675, Sections 8 and 15 accepted). There is also a pending RTO-GENESIS (class 42) and OWNLY RTO SOFTWARE (class 42). This makes public use of 'RTO' as a software name more risky than the research says. Sources: https://tsdr.uspto.gov/statusview/sn79191685 and https://tsdr.uspto.gov/statusview/sn87281675

The research missed personal-CRM competitors that already do per-person capture over time plus a pre-meeting brief. Dex sends a 'pre-meeting brief email' with attendees, past interactions and notes (article updated 2026-07-07): https://getdex.com/blog/personal-crm-for-networking/. Keep AI - Personal CRM (iOS) turns voice notes into a timeline per person with reminders, keeps data on-device and costs $7.99/mo: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/keep-ai-personal-crm/id6751458016. Reach and Contact Journal are also in this space. These are closer rivals than several of the near-name apps the research listed.

The research missed AI rehearsal and roleplay apps for specific personal and work conversations: Vocal Image, Yoodli, VirtualSpeech, Prehearse, Assertr, and 'Rehearse' on iOS. The Sep 2026 roundup that lists them is https://www.vocalimage.app/en/articles/37-practice-difficult-conversations-ai-apps/. They compete for the same 'prepare for a hard conversation' intent from the rehearsal side. Positioning should either separate RTO from them (capture over time plus a brief at talk time) or plan a roleplay mode.

Fellow is not the only work 1:1 incumbent. 15Five lets either participant add talking points before the meeting and generates talking-point recommendations with Manager Copilot (https://success.15five.com/hc/en-us/articles/50988591607835-Hold-a-1-on-1-meeting). Lattice and Hypercontext also run shared 1:1 agendas. The work-conversation niche is more crowded than the research says.

The trademark sweep for the recommended names covered only US exact-wordmark searches. There was no EUIPO, UKIPO or WIPO Global Brand Database check, no phonetic or design-mark analysis, and no check of Claude plugin marketplaces or MCP registries for name collisions (e.g. an existing 'talkahead' or 'rto' skill or connector).

The research recommends TalkAhead without noting that talkahead.com has been held since 2009 with client locks, so the .com is probably unobtainable. It also missed that beforewetalk.com was re-registered on 2026-08-26 and is being resold rather than simply lapsed.

The research checked Mulled only against app stores. USPTO shows live MULLED-containing marks only in food and beverage classes (MULLEDPOP class 30, MULLED CIDER class 3, etc.), none in software, so its conflict level is low on this evidence.

The 'do nothing' substitutes are missing from the landscape: a Claude or ChatGPT Project per person, voice roleplay in ChatGPT, and Apple's built-in 'Hold That Thought' capture shortcut. A solo MVP competes most directly with these.

I found nothing that refutes the name research: all 19 claims I checked are confirmed. The core recommendation holds. Keep RTO as an internal codename only, and rename before anything public. TalkAhead is still the lowest-conflict public name.

Independent checks, including direct USPTO tmsearch queries the original agent could not run, strengthen the findings:
- **TalkAhead:** the only US record is the TALKAHEAD registration, cancelled in 2016. There are no live filings, and no app of that name on the US App Store or US Google Play. talkahead.app is still unregistered according to registry RDAP. talkahead.com has been held with client locks since 2009.
- **Other names:** USPTO shows no RANDOM THOUGHTS mark that is still active, and no filings for THOUGHT ORGANIZER or BEFORE WE TALK.
- **Competitors:** the listings for mathaka, Talk Topics, Talkfolio, Difficult Conversation Planner, Random Thoughts Journal, Hold That Thought, PrepTalk, pocketbrief, TalkBrief, Parley, TalkTree and RTO Pro all check out, including dates, download counts and prices. Fellow's Aug 6, 2026 announcement about generating agendas through its MCP server is confirmed.

Minor corrections and nuances:
- GitHub 'thought organizer' gives 1,803 results only as an unquoted search. The exact phrase gives 97.
- beforewetalk.com is being resold (re-registered 2026-08-26), not simply lapsed.
- The Apple 'Hold That Thought' shortcut is confirmed by Apple's May 2025 newsroom post.

The most decision-relevant omissions:
1. The research never checked for existing RTO marks, and there are live US registrations for 'RTO' in class 9 (Rohde & Schwarz; 360training.com) plus pending class 42 RTO filings. That strengthens the rename advice.
2. It missed personal-CRM tools that already do capture per person plus a pre-meeting brief: Dex pre-meeting brief emails and Keep AI voice notes.
3. It missed AI conversation-rehearsal apps: Vocal Image, Prehearse, Rehearse, Yoodli.
4. It missed other work 1:1 incumbents besides Fellow: 15Five with Manager Copilot talking points, Lattice, Hypercontext.

The market gap for combining personal and work conversations, with capture over time, branching prep and a brief at talk time, still looks real. It is narrower than the research claims.

research.whitespace:
Nobody makes the intended conversation itself (me talking with this person, soon, about this) the main thing the product tracks. The market splits into six groups, and each covers one piece of RTO's job:
(1) AI meeting assistants (Granola Briefs, Fireflies Meeting Prep, Read AI, Fellow, Spinach). Their pre-meeting briefs are built from recorded history, email and the web. They need a calendar event and usually a work or external meeting: Granola's briefs are external-only, need the Business plan and Google Calendar, and are skipped when there's little context. None of them captures what you want to say.
(2) Personal CRMs (Mesh/Clay, Dex, Monica, folk) and indie 'remember people' apps (GetBriefed, RapportBuddy, mathaka). They store facts about the other person, not your goals, branches and contingencies. RapportBuddy has a talking-points list but it's manual and has no AI.
(3) Voice-capture apps (AudioPen, Voicenotes, Cleft, Letterly, TalkNotes, Pocket, Plaud). They turn rambling into clean standalone notes. The notes don't pile up by person or conversation or merge into one evolving plan.
(4) Second brains (Mem, Reflect, Capacities, Notion, Obsidian) and mind maps (Xmind, Whimsical, Heptabase, MindNode). They could hold such a plan, but only if you build it yourself, and nothing brings it up at the moment you start talking. Tana has left personal notes and become a team meeting platform.
(5) Rehearsal tools (Tough Tongue, Peopling). You practice delivery, but your agenda isn't saved and there's nothing to glance at during the real conversation.
(6) Claude-native pieces (built-in memory and Projects, the memory MCP server, Basic Memory, a community 'Difficult Conversations' skill). These are raw materials, not a workflow.
The unowned loop is: capture scattered thoughts over days by voice or chat, sort them automatically into a person plus an upcoming conversation, have AI expand them into a branching plan (goal, must-say, questions, if-they-say-X-then-Y, objections, concessions and walk-away, tone), shrink that to a glanceable checklist at conversation time (including in-person and unscheduled talks and personal ones like a spouse, contractor or friend), then run a short debrief that marks what got covered, carries open items to the next conversation and creates follow-ups.
Personal and sensitive conversations are underserved. Most tools send a bot to the meeting or record it, and are sold to teams. A private, local-first planner that never records the other person is an open position.
Platform gaps: many of the closest niche apps are Apple-only (GetBriefed, RapportBuddy, Cleft, MindNode, Talking Points, Voicethoughts). A Windows and Claude-first path isn't contested.
Naming: 'Random Thought Organizer' sits in a crowded generic space (Random Thoughts Journal, Voicethoughts, Mindscope 'Thought Organizer', Brain Dump) and doesn't describe the real benefit, which is prep for a specific conversation. 'RTO' already commonly means return-to-office and recovery time objective. I didn't find a product using the exact name, but it will be hard to search for and to trademark.
Evidence caveats: Firecrawl was out of credits, so every check used WebFetch and WebSearch. UpHabit (site returned 503, App Store page 404) and mathaka (Play Store page couldn't be parsed) are unverified. Letterly's $99/yr and MindNode's about $2.99/mo come from third-party pages and may be out of date. Fireflies' prices come from its own blog, not its pricing page.
differentiationIdeas: Conversation-first data model: Person -> Conversation (upcoming, with a status) -> Thought fragments -> Plan tree (Goal, Must-say, Questions, If-they-say-X-then-Y cards, Objections and responses, Concessions and walk-away, Tone notes) -> Outcome and follow-ups. No competitor treats the planned conversation as the main object.

Intent-first, not history-first: briefs come from your own thinking, gathered over days, and work for a first conversation, an unscheduled one or a personal one. That's the opposite of Granola, Fireflies and Read AI, which need earlier recordings or a calendar event.

Capture anywhere with automatic routing: Pocket recordings (the MCP connector is already present), Claude chat ('note for Mike: ask about the raise timeline'), email-to-self, or phone dictation. AI assigns each fragment to the right person and conversation and asks when it's unsure.

Interview mode: before a conversation, Claude asks you targeted questions ('What if they say no?', 'What's your fallback?', 'What do you need them to commit to?') to bring up forgotten branches. This turns the community 'difficult conversation' frameworks into a structured plan you keep.

A brief you can read at a glance: one screen or card with the top 3 must-says, a question checklist and if-then cards. Works on phone, desktop or on paper, ticked off during the talk and hidden once done (as Granola does). Live coverage tracking like Talking Points can come later.

60-second debrief loop: a short voice debrief after the conversation marks items covered or not covered, carries unresolved items to the next conversation with that person, and creates tasks or events through the Trello and Google Calendar connectors the user already has.

Private and local-first by default: Markdown or SQLite on the user's machine, no bot, and the other person is never recorded. This fits spouse, manager-conflict and contractor-dispute conversations that team meeting tools don't serve. Add encryption before any cloud sync.

Claude-native distribution first: a Skill plus a local MCP server means no UI to build and immediate use in Claude Desktop and Claude Code. The Markdown files stay compatible with Obsidian and Basic Memory, so moving later to a hosted MCP connector, a mobile app or a bigger product doesn't require a data migration.

Personal and work contexts in one place, with relationship-aware tone guidance (for example 'with your spouse, lead with the shared goal'). The team-sold tools (Fellow, Lattice, Range, Spinach) can't do this.
Rename around the core benefit (conversation prep and 'never forget what you meant to say') rather than 'random thoughts'. That avoids the crowded brain-dump space and the RTO abbreviation clash.
featureIdeasToBorrow: Granola Briefs: keep briefs very short (2-3 bullets up front, expandable), prepare them ahead of time (overnight), hide them once read, and don't generate one when there isn't enough substance.
Fireflies Meeting Prep and Read AI 'walk in ready': automatically carry open action items and unresolved questions from the last conversation with the same person into the next plan.
Talking Points: live check-off of points as you cover them, using on-device speech recognition and matching on meaning. Start with manual tick boxes in the MVP and add live tracking in a later phase.
Cleft and AudioPen: 'append and continue' onto an existing note, custom output styles with a choice of rewrite strength, and on-device transcription for privacy.
Mem Push-to-Remember: a hotkey or single-button voice capture where the agent decides which plan the thought belongs to and when to bring it back, plus proactive nudges before a known conversation.
GetBriefed: a daily dashboard of who you'll talk to today with suggested topics, and reminders that expire for follow-ups.

Official memory MCP server and Basic Memory: the entity, relation and observation model for people, with Markdown files as the source of truth plus a searchable index, which gives an easy migration path to Obsidian or a hosted backend.
Xmind and Whimsical AI: one-click 'expand this branch' on any plan node to generate sub-questions, objections or contingencies.
Tough Tongue AI and Peopling: an optional 'rehearse this plan' mode where Claude plays the other person, using the objections from your plan.

Pocket MCP and Voicenotes: OAuth for any remote connector, clearly split read and write tools, and a tool set that's the same regardless of plan tier, as a pattern for RTO's own connector and its security review.

Wispr Flow Notetaker (Aug 2026, Windows since Sep 15, 2026) is missing: briefs from your own notes plus the web, with MCP. It is the most direct contender on Windows for 'briefs from your own notes' (https://wisprflow.ai/post/wispr-flow-notetaker).

Big-platform meeting prep is missing: Microsoft 365 Copilot meeting prep (needs Copilot seats and admin-enabled Meeting Insights, per hirekai.ai, Sep 16, 2026: https://hirekai.ai/blog/ai-meeting-prep), Google Gemini meeting prep and Daily Brief (third-party sources only, not verified first-party), and ChatGPT Pulse. A search snippet from help.openai.com says Pulse is being retired and folded into scheduled tasks; the page returned 403, so that's unverified. A user could build a DIY RTO from ChatGPT or Gemini memory plus scheduled tasks.

Granola's Android app (July 1, 2026) and in-person capture aren't mentioned, and neither is its MCP (on Business). Together they reduce the 'in-person, unscheduled' gap RTO is claimed to own (https://releasebot.io/updates/granola).
Tana Outliner still exists as a personal outliner with mobile apps and voice input (https://outliner.tana.inc). The research implies Tana has no personal-notes product at all.

Claude platform limits that affect the 'Skill plus local MCP, capture anywhere' recommendation: (a) Official docs list custom remote-MCP connectors for Claude web, Cowork and Desktop, call installing connectors on mobile 'beta', and describe Desktop and web as the primary path. Free plans get only one custom connector (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11176164-use-connectors-to-extend-claude-s-capabilities). (b) A local desktop extension (MCPB) runs only in Claude Desktop, so capture from the phone needs an internet-reachable remote MCP server with OAuth. (c) MCP tunnels, which would let Claude reach a private server without exposing it, are an Enterprise-only research preview (https://claude.com/docs/connectors/mcp-tunnels/overview). (d) Skills work on Free through Enterprise but need code execution, and the docs don't say whether they run on mobile (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512180-use-skills-in-claude).

No trademark search (USPTO TESS/EUIPO) or domain or app-store name availability check was done for either the current name or a replacement. The naming advice rests on web and app-store searches only.

Gating details that matter when using these tools as RTO inputs were left out: AudioPen's MCP needs the Prime tier, and Pocket's MCP includes a write tool (update_pocket_actionitem). Both are relevant to the security review and to the 'read-only input' assumption.

hirekai.ai (Sep 2026) points out that every automated brief tool needs a calendar invite, so calls set up over Slack get no brief. That supports RTO's case for unscheduled conversations and wasn't cited (https://hirekai.ai/blog/ai-meeting-prep).
verification.summary: I checked 22 of the claims most likely to change decisions. 13 hold up as stated or with small fixes, 7 are wrong or incomplete, and 1 couldn't be checked; the 22nd, on the name, holds up but trademark availability is still unchecked. The core picture stands: Granola Briefs (external meetings only, Business plan plus Google Calendar, launched May 2026), GetBriefed, RapportBuddy, Talking Points, Mesh/Automattic, the memory and connector features of AudioPen, Voicenotes, Pocket, Read AI and Monica, Fireflies Meeting Prep, the reference memory MCP server and Basic Memory. Several corrections matter for decisions. (1) The whitespace claim is overstated. SayIt already writes a plan for one conversation, including the three most likely replies with prepared answers, plus roleplay. Wispr Flow Notetaker (on Windows since September 2026, with MCP) builds briefs from your own notes. What stays open is the loop across several days: capture on the go, attach to a person and conversation, glanceable brief, debrief. (2) Granola now has an Android app for in-person meetings. (3) Tana still runs Tana Outliner as a personal notes tool. (4) Claude memory is available on the Free plan too, not only paid plans. (5) Otter's Enterprise Sales Agent does do pre-call briefs. Smaller fixes: Read AI's 5-license minimum is on Enterprise+, Voicenotes supports 100+ languages, AudioPen's MCP needs Prime, and Pocket's MCP includes a write tool. mathaka's details couldn't be verified. No product uses the exact name 'Random Thought Organizer', but no trademark search was done. Key platform omissions for the delivery plan: a local desktop extension only works in Claude Desktop, and connectors on mobile are beta, so capturing from the phone needs a remote MCP server with OAuth. MCP tunnels, which would avoid exposing that server to the internet, are Enterprise-only. Firecrawl had no credits left, so every check used WebFetch and WebSearch. The Play Store pages and the OpenAI help center page couldn't be opened.

keyFacts.claim: Claude Skills load on claude.ai web, Claude Code CLI, Claude desktop app, and sync to local machines when you sign in
Skills persist within a session's context window but do not automatically persist memory between sessions unless using Claude Projects or Managed Agents memory stores
Claude Code Plugins bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and load on Terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, Claude desktop app, and cloud/web sessions
MCP servers run locally (stdio) or remotely (HTTP/SSE/WebSocket); local servers work in Code, cloud sessions, desktop app, and Agent SDK; remote servers require OAuth 2.0 or fixed headers
Claude mobile apps (iOS/Android) support cloud sessions and Remote Control, but not native Claude Code plugins or local MCP servers
Claude Managed Agents is in public beta with cloud sandbox + optional self-hosted sandboxes on Cloudflare, Daytona, Modal, or Vercel; memory stores persist across sessions
Managed Agents memory stores are mounted as `/mnt/memory/` directories, support up to 10,000 memories per store, and create immutable versions for audit trails with 30-day retention

Claude Agent SDK (Python `claude-agent-sdk`, TypeScript `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) bundles built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch) and runs on your own infrastructure
Custom connectors on claude.ai work on Free (1 connector), Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans; they do not work in native mobile apps (only in web/cloud sessions)
Desktop Extensions (.mcpb) install local MCP servers in Claude Desktop only; they do not work on web, mobile, or Claude Code CLI
Claude Projects are in public beta on Pro and Max plans, allowing Claude to coordinate parallel cloud sessions with shared context and memory
Managed Agents pricing: standard Claude API token rates + $0.08/active session-hour (first 50 hours/day free) + $10 per 1,000 web searches
Agent SDK on subscription plans draws from a separate monthly Agent SDK credit pool; API key usage bills per token as usual
Tool Runner (client.beta.messages.tool_runner) loops over tools you define with per-turn hooks for approval, error interception, and retries—no built-in tools, minimal harness
Managed Agents sessions are not eligible for Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or HIPAA BAA due to stateful session persistence; user control remains via API delete

options.name: Claude Skill (claude.ai + Claude Code CLI)
options.whereItRuns: Claude.ai web, Claude Code (Terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, Desktop app), cloud sessions. Mobile: not directly; Remote Control can reference it.
options.persistence: Within session context only. No cross-session memory. If you upgrade to Projects (beta), memory persists via project-level conversation state.
options.mobileAccess: No. Mobile app only supports cloud sessions and Remote Control, which reference skills from your main account but don't run them natively.
options.installFriction: Low. Create `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in your repo or `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` locally. Invoke with `/<skill-name>`. No marketplace install needed for personal use.
options.buildEffort: Very low. Markdown + YAML frontmatter. Static content + command injection. 1–2 hours for a working RTO skill.
options.securityConsiderations: Runs as you in claude.ai. No isolation. Markdown files checked into git are versioned. Invocation requires explicit `disable-model-invocation` or `user-invocable` controls.
options.migrationPath: Can be packaged into a Claude Code Plugin later. Can also seed an MCP server for remote access. Not directly portable to Managed Agents (no skill format there).
options.limitations: No persistent data between sessions. No automatic background execution. No mobile native support. Context-only memory.

options.name: Claude Code Plugin (skills + MCP server bundle)
options.whereItRuns: Claude Code: Terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, Desktop app, cloud sessions. Claude.ai: skills only (no MCP servers, agents, hooks). Mobile: via synced account but not native execution.
options.persistence: Plugin components (skills, agents, MCP servers) load per session. No cross-session persistence. Sessions share context within one chat.
options.mobileAccess: Skills sync to mobile app but do not run there. MCP servers do not sync to mobile.
options.installFriction: Medium. Create plugin.json manifest, organize skills/agents/MCP in folders, publish to marketplace or install with `--plugin-dir`. Marketplace install is one command; custom marketplace requires URL.
options.buildEffort: Low–medium. Package skills (1–2 hrs), write MCP server for Trello/Gmail/Calendar connector (4–8 hrs with FastMCP/MCP SDK), test with `--plugin-dir`. Total: 8–16 hours.
options.securityConsiderations: Skills + MCP servers run with your permissions. MCP can access external APIs (require OAuth or API keys stored in Claude config). Trust the marketplace source (Anthropic reviews official directory submissions).
options.migrationPath: Easier than standalone. Can evolve to Managed Agents by exporting the MCP server config. Can also add a custom connector to claude.ai if only remote API is needed.
options.limitations: No native mobile execution. MCP servers don't work on mobile. No persistent memory between sessions without separate storage (local DB, cloud service). Context limited to session.

options.name: MCP Server (local or remote HTTP)
options.whereItRuns: Local (stdio): Claude Code CLI, desktop app (with `~/.claude/mcp.json`), Agent SDK, cloud sessions. Remote (HTTP): claude.ai (via custom connector), Code, Agent SDK, Managed Agents.
options.persistence: MCP tool calls are stateless. Persistence must be implemented in your MCP server (file I/O, database, external API). No automatic session replay.
options.mobileAccess: Remote HTTP servers: only via claude.ai custom connectors (Free=1, Pro/Max=unlimited). No native mobile MCP support.
options.installFriction: Low–medium. Local: edit `~/.claude/mcp.json` or use `claude mcp add`. Remote: add custom connector URL in claude.ai. Auth: OAuth 2.0 or fixed headers (beta).
options.buildEffort: Medium–high. Build MCP server with FastMCP (Python, 4–8 hrs) or MCP SDK (Node.js, 6–10 hrs). Define tools for thought capture, expansion, conversation retrieval, export. Local testing: 2–4 hrs.
options.securityConsiderations: Local: runs as you, access to filesystem/shell. Remote: requires HTTPS, OAuth recommended for multi-user. Anthropic reviews directory submissions. Private/internal servers: use MCP Tunnels (beta) for secure private endpoint.
options.migrationPath: Excellent migration path. MCP servers are composable with Plugins, Managed Agents, and Agent SDK. If moving to Managed Agents, server config reuses directly.
options.limitations: Stateless by default. No built-in memory between turns. Requires your own backend for persistent storage. Remote servers must be internet-accessible (unless using MCP Tunnels). No mobile native support.

options.name: Desktop Extension (.mcpb local MCP bundle)
options.whereItRuns: Claude Desktop app only (Windows, macOS, Linux). Not in web, mobile, or Claude Code CLI.
options.persistence: Depends on the bundled MCP server implementation. No automatic persistence in the extension itself.
options.installFriction: Low. Drag-and-drop `.mcpb` file into **Settings > Extensions** in Claude Desktop. Organization: enterprise software management (MDM) distribution.
options.buildEffort: Medium–high. Build MCP server in Python/Node.js (4–8 hrs), package with MCPB tool, test locally. Total: 8–12 hours.
options.securityConsiderations: Runs locally with your user permissions. Audit as a native desktop process. No network dependency unless MCP server calls external APIs. Enterprise: full MDM control.
options.migrationPath: Can extract MCP server from MCPB and deploy as remote HTTP server to migrate to web/mobile. Not a natural path to Managed Agents (no MCPB equivalent there).
options.limitations: Desktop-only. No mobile, web, or CLI access. Requires distribution via file or enterprise management for teams. MCPB is a local packaging format, not a marketplace.

options.name: Claude Projects (beta, zero-code persistence)
options.whereItRuns: Web (claude.ai/code) and Claude desktop app (Code tab). Mobile app via Remote Control. Cloud sessions coordinate parallel threads.
options.persistence: Projects persist conversation threads and shared context across multiple sessions. Claude coordinates parallel work. Memory is at the project level, not per-agent.
options.mobileAccess: View progress on mobile app. Full editing in web or desktop app Code tab. Cloud threads continue after you close the laptop.
options.installFriction: Very low. Start a project from `claude.ai/code` (Pro/Max only), describe goals, let Claude create threads. No coding, no setup.
options.buildEffort: Zero. Define problem statement once; Claude orchestrates. Good for: iterative refinement, collecting scattered thoughts, letting Claude coordinate background work.
options.securityConsiderations: Cloud-hosted by Anthropic. No code or MCP to review. Standard claude.ai security. Files and context are in your workspace.
options.migrationPath: Projects are read-only for now; cannot export to Managed Agents or Agent SDK. Intended for: exploratory work, team coordination, not production automation.
options.limitations: Beta feature (rolling out Pro/Max). No API access. No scheduled execution. No custom tool integration (no MCP, no plugins). Claude decides task delegation; you coordinate threads.

options.name: Custom Connector on claude.ai (remote MCP server URL)
options.whereItRuns: claude.ai web, Claude desktop app, Cowork, cloud sessions. Mobile web (claude.ai on phone) only. Not native mobile app or Claude Code CLI.
options.persistence: Connector executes tool calls; persistence depends on your backend server. No session state in claude.ai itself.
options.mobileAccess: Browser-based only (claude.ai/mobile). No native iOS/Android app support for custom connectors.
options.installFriction: Very low. Add connector URL in **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector**. Choose OAuth or no-sign-in. No installation required.

options.name: Claude Managed Agents (cloud sandbox + persistent sessions)

options.persistence: Sessions persist 30 days+ (on demand storage). Memory stores mounted as `/mnt/memory/` directories with up to 10,000 memories per store. Versions kept 30 days (audit trail).
options.mobileAccess: Via REST API only; no mobile app native integration yet.
options.installFriction: Medium. Create agent (model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers) and environment (cloud or self-hosted). Deploy sessions via API. CLI: `ant` command available.

options.migrationPath: Excellent. Managed Agents is the long-term production service. MCP servers, memory stores, and scheduled deployments are forward-looking. Natural next step from Agent SDK or custom connectors.

options.name: Claude Agent SDK (self-hosted harness with built-in tools)
options.whereItRuns: Your infrastructure: Python or TypeScript application on any server, laptop, container, VM. You manage deployment, scaling, and persistence.
options.persistence: Agent loop maintains session state. Sessions can be saved/resumed by capturing session_id. Implement your own storage (database, files) for cross-session memory.
options.mobileAccess: Build your own mobile client (web API, mobile app) that calls your Agent SDK service. No native mobile harness.
options.installFriction: Low. `pip install claude-agent-sdk` (Python 3.10+) or `npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` (Node.js). Binaries bundled; no separate install.

options.securityConsiderations: You own security. Built-in tools (Bash, web fetch) are high-trust; configure carefully. Integrate with your auth, rate limiting, and audit logs.
options.migrationPath: Good intermediate step. Managed Agents is the upgrade path for long-running async work; Tool Runner is the downgrade for fine-grained control.
options.limitations: You operate it. No sandbox guarantee (depends on your deployment). You handle scaling, persistence, error recovery, monitoring. Not a managed service.

options.name: Messages API + Tool Runner (fine-grained control)
options.whereItRuns: Your code, any language via HTTP API. Full control over loop, tools, persistence.
options.persistence: You build it. Manage conversation history, implement memory, handle session state.
options.mobileAccess: Build your own client (web API, mobile app, CLI).
options.installFriction: Medium. Use any SDK (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, C#, PHP, Ruby) or raw HTTP. Tool Runner is a helper (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) that loops for you.
options.buildEffort: High. Build agent loop, define every tool, implement approval gates, error handling, streaming, storage. 16–40 hours for a production agent.
options.securityConsiderations: You build and own security. No built-in tools; define custom tools carefully. You implement approval workflows, rate limiting, and audit.
options.migrationPath: Tool Runner → Agent SDK (add built-in tools, simplified loop). Agent SDK → Managed Agents (move to managed execution). Not a migration path for RTO (overkill in reverse).

research.recommendationNotes:
## Recommended Path for Random Thought Organizer (RTO)

**Phase 1 (Week 1–2): Prototype with Claude Skill**
Start with a simple Claude Skill in your `.claude/skills/rto/SKILL.md`. This gives you immediate testing in claude.ai without any deployment:
- Define prompt to guide thought capture (free-form text, structure with branches)
- Use command injection (`!bash`) to timestamp entries, save to local files
- Load and expand prior thoughts with bash + grep to retrieve old session content
- Zero friction; rapid iteration

**Phase 2 (Week 2–3): Add Connectors with MCP Server**
Build a lightweight MCP server (FastMCP, Python, 4–6 hrs) to:
- Read from Google Calendar (fetch conversation participants, upcoming events)
- Query Gmail (extract prior email threads with that person)
- Query Trello (pull context from person's board if exists)
- Parse captured thoughts into structured format (person, meeting date, discussion paths, questions)

Deploy as:
- **Local (CLI)**: In Claude Code with `~/.claude/mcp.json` for your own use
- **Remote (HTTP)**: Custom connector in claude.ai for easy access

**Phase 3 (Week 4–6): Persistent State with Managed Agents (Production)**
Once you've proven the concept:
- Create Managed Agents agent with:
  - Your MCP server as a configured tool
  - System prompt that expands/challenges thoughts
  - Memory store (`memstore_...`) per person for thought history
- Deploy session-based API endpoint for recurring use
- Each conversation with a person gets a session; memory persists across meetings

**Why this path:**
1. **Fast validation**: Skill = testable in hours
2. **Real integration**: MCP server connects to your actual tools (Calendar, Gmail, Trello)
3. **Scalable persistence**: Managed Agents memory stores handle 10k+ thoughts per person without you managing DB
4. **Low infrastructure**: Anthropic manages sandbox; you own the MCP server (4 small API wrappers)

## Alternative (Fast-Track)

If you want **persistent storage immediately** without building an MCP server:
- Use **Claude Projects (beta)** on claude.ai to capture + expand thoughts iteratively
- No coding; Claude auto-orchestrates refinement threads
- Not a standalone product, but sufficient for personal use (capture thoughts → Projects session → export as markdown/JSON afterward)

## Do Not Start With

- **Messages API + Tool Runner**: Overkill; you'd build a full agent loop from scratch. Skip unless you need <100ms latency or extreme fine-grained control.
- **Desktop Extension (.mcpb)**: Desktop-only; blocks mobile access. Only if you need zero-internet offline capability.
- **Claude Code Plugin (Phase 1)**: Skip the packaging step until Phase 2. Use a bare skill first.

## Security & Data Notes

- **Thoughts are private**: With Managed Agents self-hosted sandboxes or local MCP, your thoughts never leave your infrastructure unless you explicitly sync them
- **Google Calendar/Gmail/Trello**: Use OAuth for auth; Anthropic does NOT see your data. MCP server runs on your machine (local) or your infrastructure (self-hosted)
- **Branching & Testing**: Use git branches for MCP server iterations (`feature/gmail-search`, `feature/calendar-fetch`). Evals (`claude plugin eval`) for plugin correctness before release

---

## Interview Questions for You (to refine further)

I've outlined the path above based on the documented capabilities. To finalize, answer:

1. **Timing**: How soon do you need RTO usable? (1 week = Skill only; 3 weeks = Skill + MCP; 6+ weeks = full Managed Agents)
2. **Data scope**: Do you want thoughts stored on your machine, or synced to a cloud service (Supabase, Firebase)? Privacy requirement?
3. **Mobile requirement**: Do you need to *capture* thoughts on mobile (voice memo + transcribe), or just review on mobile? Capture needs different architecture (webhook to your MCP server).
4. **Integration depth**: Must RTO auto-pull conversation history from prior email/calendar with that person, or manual paste-in okay?
5. **Team**: Solo product, or shared tool with spouse/manager? (Affects auth, data sharing, deployment model.)

checkedClaims.claim: Custom connectors on claude.ai do not work in the native iOS/Android apps, only on web and in cloud sessions. Mobile access to a remote MCP server is browser-only.
checkedClaims.correction: Once a remote (custom) connector is connected, it works in the native mobile apps. Anthropic's connector docs list 'Claude mobile app: remote connectors' and say a connected connector 'is available in your conversations on the web, desktop, and mobile.' The custom-connector help article (updated 2026-08-11) says Anthropic's cloud calls the server 'across every Claude client, including claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork, and the mobile apps.' Adding a connector from the phone is still in beta, so add it on web or desktop first. This is the most decision-relevant error: a remote MCP server gives native on-the-go capture from the phone app.

checkedClaims.claim: Custom connectors are not available in the Claude Code CLI.
checkedClaims.correction: The connectors you add in claude.ai are also available in Claude Code, both in the terminal and in cloud sessions, when you sign in with your Claude account. The same remote server can also be added directly with 'claude mcp add --transport http'.

checkedClaims.claim: Custom connectors work on Free (1 connector), Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed. On Team and Enterprise only an Owner (or an Enterprise member with a library-management role) can add one. Request-header auth is a beta limited to some organizations: up to 4 headers, and Anthropic must approve custom header names. The docs now recommend the CIMD option ('Use Claude's published identity') over Dynamic Client Registration. The server must be publicly reachable over HTTPS from Anthropic's IP ranges.

checkedClaims.claim: Claude Skill option: mobile access 'No'. Skills sync to mobile but do not run there.
checkedClaims.correction: Anthropic's plugin support table defines 'Chat' as claude.ai on web, desktop and the mobile apps, and marks Skills (and commands) as 'Loads' there. Claude Academy states: 'Conversations, projects, memory, skills, uploads, voice, and your connectors ... work the same on the web, your phone, and the desktop app.' In claude.ai, skills need code execution turned on.

checkedClaims.claim: Skills do not persist memory between sessions unless you use Claude Projects (beta) or Managed Agents memory stores. Skill limitation: 'No persistent data between sessions.'
checkedClaims.correction: claude.ai has memory across chats on Free, Pro and Max by default, and it works on mobile. Each claude.ai Project has its own separate memory space. Claude Code carries knowledge across sessions with CLAUDE.md and auto memory. A skill installed locally in Claude Code can also read and write files on disk.

checkedClaims.claim: Phase 1: test the skill immediately in claude.ai with no deployment, using '!bash' command injection to timestamp entries and save them to local files.
checkedClaims.correction: The '!`cmd`' injection is a Claude Code feature. Claude Code also refuses to run these commands for skills synced from your claude.ai account. On claude.ai a skill runs in Anthropic's code-execution sandbox, which cannot reach your local disk, and its files stay available within the conversation. Local-file persistence therefore works only for a skill installed locally in Claude Code (~/.claude/skills or the repo's .claude/skills), not 'in claude.ai'.

checkedClaims.claim: Claude Projects is in public beta on Pro and Max and coordinates parallel cloud sessions with shared context and memory.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed, with context. It is rolling out gradually with a waitlist and is not on Team or Enterprise. It is a Claude Code cloud-session coordinator built around repositories. It is not the classic claude.ai chat Projects (all plans, grouped chats plus files plus per-project memory), and that classic version is the better zero-code fit for RTO.

checkedClaims.claim: Claude Projects (beta) limitations: no scheduled execution, no custom tool integration (no MCP, no plugins), no export, and mobile only for viewing or through Remote Control.
checkedClaims.correction: Projects can create routines for scheduled work (a Routines tab). Plugins are added under Project settings > Plugins. Threads get your claude.ai connectors. You can create and use projects in the iOS and Android apps. Stated limitations are different: no terminal CLI, single user with no sharing, and threads cannot be moved between projects.

checkedClaims.claim: Skills are not directly portable to Managed Agents because it has no skill format.
checkedClaims.correction: In Managed Agents, an Agent is defined as 'The model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, and skills.' The Agent SDK also loads skills from .claude/ and ~/.claude/. A skill-first design therefore carries across Claude Code, claude.ai, the Agent SDK and Managed Agents.

checkedClaims.claim: Managed Agents is in public beta, with optional self-hosted sandboxes on Cloudflare, Daytona, Modal or Vercel.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed. It needs the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header. The provider list is longer: AWS Lambda MicroVMs, Blaxel, E2B, Fly.io, GKE Agent Sandbox, Namespace and Superserve are also documented.

checkedClaims.claim: Managed Agents memory stores mount at /mnt/memory/, hold up to 10,000 memories per store, and create immutable versions with 30-day retention.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed, with limits the research left out. Each memory is capped at 100 kB. A session can attach at most 8 stores. Writes fail once a store reaches 10,000 memories, so the plan's '10k+ thoughts per person' is wrong for a single store. Recent versions of a live memory are kept past 30 days. Stores use a separate beta header (agent-memory-2026-07-22). Docs warn that a read_write store can be poisoned by prompt injection.

checkedClaims.claim: Managed Agents pricing: standard token rates + $0.08 per active session-hour (first 50 hours/day free) + $10 per 1,000 web searches.
checkedClaims.correction: $0.08 per session-hour and $10 per 1,000 searches are correct. The official pricing page lists no free session-hour allowance, so '50 hours/day free' is unsupported. Runtime accrues only while a session's status is 'running', and idle time is not billed. The only free-hours allowance on the pricing page is for the code-execution tool, and it is per month.

checkedClaims.claim: Managed Agents sessions are not eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed ('not currently eligible'). You can delete sessions and uploaded files through the API.

checkedClaims.claim: On subscription plans the Agent SDK draws from a separate monthly Agent SDK credit pool.
checkedClaims.correction: Anthropic announced this for June 15, 2026, then paused it. The help article's June 15 update says: 'For now, nothing has changed': Agent SDK, claude -p and third-party app usage still count against subscription usage limits. The Agent SDK docs also say third-party developers may not offer claude.ai login in their products without prior approval. A standalone RTO product would therefore need API-key (per-token) billing.

checkedClaims.claim: Thoughts stay private: with Managed Agents self-hosted sandboxes or a local MCP server, they never leave your infrastructure. For Google Calendar, Gmail and Trello over OAuth, Anthropic does not see your data.
checkedClaims.correction: Self-hosted sandboxes keep orchestration on Anthropic's side, and 'Tool inputs and outputs still flow to Anthropic's control plane (where Claude runs).' Any tool result, local or remote, enters the model context that Anthropic processes. For custom connectors, Anthropic's cloud itself calls your server (support article 11175166). On consumer plans, chats are used for training only if the user opts in; otherwise the standard retention is 30 days.

checkedClaims.claim: Private or internal MCP servers can use MCP Tunnels (beta) as a secure private endpoint.
checkedClaims.correction: MCP tunnels are a research preview. On claude.ai they are available only to Enterprise-plan organizations, by request. On the API and Managed Agents they are also a limited research preview that needs an access request. A solo Pro or Max user cannot use them, so RTO's remote server must be internet-reachable and protected with OAuth.

checkedClaims.claim: Claude Code plugins on claude.ai load skills only (no MCP servers, agents or hooks). Plugins have no native mobile execution.
checkedClaims.correction: In Chat (web, desktop and mobile), a plugin's skills and commands load. Its remote http/sse MCP servers appear on the plugin's Connectors tab and work once connected. Agents, hooks and local MCP servers are ignored in Chat. Cowork loads agents and hooks.

checkedClaims.claim: Desktop Extensions (.mcpb) work only in Claude Desktop, not on web, mobile or the Claude Code CLI.
checkedClaims.correction: The direct drag-and-drop install is in the desktop app only. However, a Claude Code plugin's mcpServers key accepts a packaged .mcpb (or .dxt) file, and Anthropic's platform table marks local MCP servers 'including .mcpb bundles' as 'Loads' in Claude Code. They are ignored in web and mobile Chat.

checkedClaims.claim: MCP: local server config lives in ~/.claude/mcp.json, and remote servers require OAuth 2.0 or fixed headers.
checkedClaims.correction: Claude Code stores local and user scope in ~/.claude.json and project scope in .mcp.json at the repo root. Remote servers can be unauthenticated, or use static --header, OAuth 2.0, or a headersHelper command. Transports are stdio, HTTP, SSE (deprecated) and WebSocket.

checkedClaims.claim: Claude plugin evals ('claude plugin eval') can check plugin correctness before release.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed. 'claude plugin eval' and 'claude plugin eval init' exist; the command was added in Claude Code v2.1.269 (Sept 2026). For a standalone skill, skill-creator runs a similar comparison, but in its own evals/evals.json format, and neither tool reads the other's files. 'claude plugin validate' checks schema only.

checkedClaims.claim: Tool Runner (client.beta.messages.tool_runner) loops over your tools with per-turn hooks for approval, error interception and retries. The Messages API has no built-in tools.
checkedClaims.correction: The method exists and is in beta in 7 SDKs. The docs say the opposite about approval: 'When you need human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging, or conditional execution, use the manual loop instead.' The Messages API also has server-side tools (web search, web fetch, code execution), each priced on the pricing page.

checkedClaims.claim: The Claude mobile apps support cloud sessions and Remote Control, but not native Claude Code plugins or local MCP servers.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed in substance: the app is a client, and '/plugin' does not work from it. The research omits that Remote Control drives a session on your own machine, which does use your local MCP servers. The phone also reaches Projects and Dispatch (Dispatch needs Pro or Max). Channels (Telegram, Discord, iMessage) can hand work to your machine.

omissions: Classic claude.ai Projects plus cross-chat memory is the real zero-code MVP, and the research confused it with the Claude Code 'Projects (beta)' coordinator. Classic Projects exist on all plans with per-project memory, and memory works on Free, Pro and Max, including mobile. Anthropic's help article is https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11817273-use-claude-s-chat-search-and-memory-to-build-on-previous-context. A 'RTO' Project with instructions plus an uploaded skill is testable today on phone and web.

Phase 2 duplicates connectors the user already has. The builder already has Google Calendar, Gmail, Drive, Trello and Pocket connectors, and those also reach Claude Code (https://claude.com/docs/connectors/overview). The only new server RTO needs is its own store of people, conversations, thoughts, briefs and outcomes, not wrappers around Google or Trello.

The research missed the most direct route to capture on the go. A small remote MCP server added once as a custom connector is usable from the native phone app, the web, desktop and Claude Code (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp). Paired with a skill it gives one backend across all surfaces. The research also skipped MCP Apps, which render interactive UI such as a glanceable checklist, and which Anthropic says the mobile app can now display (March 25, 2026 release note: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12138966-release-notes).

A remote connector triggers the user's security-review requirement, and the research understated this. The server must be reachable over the public internet from Anthropic's IP ranges, use HTTPS, and should use OAuth (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp). MCP tunnels are not an option below Enterprise. The research also did not cover threat modeling for prompt injection from email or calendar content written into the thought store (see the Managed Agents memory warning: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory).

Other mobile-capture paths were not assessed: voice mode, the Pocket recorder connector, Dispatch (Pro/Max), Channels via Telegram, Discord or iMessage (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile.md), and routines, scheduled cloud runs that could prepare a pre-meeting brief (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-projects.md).

Consumer privacy settings are missing. On Free, Pro and Max, chats and coding sessions are used for training only if the user opts in, and Incognito chats are never used (https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023580-is-my-data-used-for-model-training). Retention is 30 days, or up to 5 years de-identified if the user opts in (https://www.anthropic.com/news/updates-to-our-consumer-terms, not opened directly; the retention figures came from a search result summary). This matters for thoughts about named third parties such as a spouse or manager.

Productization constraints are missing. Agent SDK products may not offer claude.ai login without approval (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview), so a standalone app means API-key billing. Distributing a plugin or connector to other users also means per-user OAuth and multi-tenant data isolation.

GitHub plan limits that bear on the user's branching, testing and security-review requirement are absent. Protected branches and required reviewers on private repos need GitHub Pro or higher (https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans). Code scanning on private repos needs a GitHub Code Security license (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/code-scanning/introduction-to-code-scanning/about-code-scanning). Rulesets are described for Team and Enterprise plans.
The research never mentions Cowork. Cowork loads plugins' agents and hooks, and local MCP servers when the session runs on your computer (https://claude.com/docs/plugins/platform-support).
This platform research makes no name, trademark or competitor claims, so the 'RTO' name review and the competitor scan still need their own verification track.
verification.summary:
I checked 22 claims against official Anthropic, Claude and GitHub docs. 6 are confirmed, often with added caveats, and 16 are refuted.

**What changes the plan**
- **Mobile works.** The research's biggest error is saying custom connectors and skills do not work in the native mobile apps. Anthropic's docs say remote (custom) connectors work on web, desktop, the mobile apps and Claude Code once connected, and skills load in mobile chat. A skill plus one small remote MCP server, added as a custom connector, therefore covers phone capture, web, desktop and Claude Code from a single backend.
- **Phase 1 as written won't run.** Using '!' command injection to save to local files is a Claude Code-only feature. Claude Code also refuses to run it for skills synced from your claude.ai account, and a claude.ai skill runs in a sandbox that can't reach your disk.
- **The zero-code option is misidentified.** Claude Projects (beta) is a coordinator for Claude Code cloud sessions. Its listed limits are wrong: it supports routines, plugins, connectors and mobile. The zero-code MVP the research missed is a classic claude.ai Project with cross-chat memory, which exists on all plans and works on mobile.
- **Skills carry over to Managed Agents.** The claim that skills can't move to Managed Agents is wrong: an agent there is defined as model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills.

**Wrong facts that affect cost or security**
- The separate monthly Agent SDK credit pool was paused on June 15, 2026. Agent SDK use still counts against the subscription.
- Managed Agents has no '50 free hours/day'. The $0.08 per session-hour and $10 per 1,000 web searches are correct.
- MCP tunnels are a research preview, available on claude.ai only to Enterprise organizations by request. A solo developer can't use them.
- The privacy statements ('thoughts never leave your infrastructure', 'Anthropic does NOT see your data') are false. Tool inputs and outputs reach Anthropic, and custom connectors are called from Anthropic's cloud. The server must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, and OAuth is advised, so it falls under the user's security-review requirement.
- Smaller errors: the MCP config path is `~/.claude.json` or `.mcp.json`, not `~/.claude/mcp.json`. `.mcpb` bundles do load in Claude Code through plugins. Tool Runner's docs send human approval to the manual loop instead.

**Confirmed**
- Custom connector plan availability (Free gets one).
- Managed Agents beta status, memory store limits (10,000 memories per store, 100 kB each, 8 stores per session), and no ZDR/HIPAA eligibility.
- `claude plugin eval` exists.
- The Claude Code mobile limitations.

**Suggested path**
Skip building wrappers for Google Calendar, Gmail and Trello; the user already has those connectors. Build one RTO store as:
1. A local Claude Code skill writing markdown to a git repo, or a claude.ai Project with memory.
2. The same skill plus a small OAuth-protected remote MCP server as a custom connector, for phone and web.
3. The same skill and server moved into Managed Agents or the Agent SDK later.

research.branchingRecommendation:
RECOMMENDATION: GitHub Flow, run in the trunk-based style: one protected `main`, short-lived branches, a PR for every change, and delete the branch after merge. Do NOT use Git Flow.

WHY
- Branches should last "a couple of days"; beyond two days they risk becoming long-lived feature branches. Use one developer per branch and merge through a PR after CI (https://trunkbaseddevelopment.com/short-lived-feature-branches/).
- GitHub Flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow with descriptive branch names and deletion after merge (https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow).
- Git Flow's own author, in a note dated March 5, 2020, recommends a simpler workflow such as GitHub Flow for continuously delivered software. He keeps Git Flow for explicitly versioned software with several supported versions (https://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/). If you later must maintain an old major line, for example a v1 local stdio server alongside a v2 remote server, cut a `release/v1` branch at that point rather than adopting Git Flow up front.

ISSUE-LINKED BRANCHES
- Every change starts from a GitHub issue. Create the branch with `gh issue develop 42 --name fix/42-brief-drops-followups --checkout`. It records the branch as linked to the issue, and `--base` sets the PR base (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_develop).
- Naming convention: `<type>/<issue#>-<kebab-slug>`, where type is one of feat|fix|sec|test|docs|chore|refactor|perf|ci. Use `sec/` for security fixes so they stand out. Enforce it with a regex in a pre-push hook and in a CI job, because branch-name rulesets are not available on private Free repos.
- The PR description carries `Closes #42`. The issue then closes automatically when the PR merges into the default branch (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue).

COMMITS AND RELEASES
- Use Conventional Commits 1.0.0 in the form `<type>[optional scope]: <description>`. `fix` maps to PATCH, `feat` to MINOR, and `BREAKING CHANGE` or `!` to MAJOR (https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). Squash-merge PRs and make the PR title the conventional commit, so `main` stays linear and parseable.
- Scopes to use: skill, mcp, store, brief, auth, ci.
- Treat MCP tool contract changes as MAJOR: renaming or removing a tool, or a breaking change to inputSchema or outputSchema. Clients and Claude cache tool lists, and the 2026-07-28 spec adds ttlMs caching.
- Release automation: use release-please through googleapis/release-please-action. It keeps a Release PR up to date from the conventional commits, and merging that PR updates the CHANGELOG, tags the version and creates a GitHub Release. It supports node and python release types and manifest mode for several packages in one repo (https://github.com/googleapis/release-please). This fits a solo developer best because it needs no extra per-PR files.
- Choose Changesets instead only if you end up publishing several npm packages from a pnpm workspace and want explicit per-change release notes. It is monorepo-focused and does not depend on commit messages. Its main branch is v3 development and stable is maintenance/v2; npm latest is @changesets/cli 3.0.3 (https://github.com/changesets/changesets).

SERVER-SIDE PROTECTION: DECIDE REPO VISIBILITY FIRST
(a) Public repo. Only code goes in the repo, never user notes. You get rulesets, required checks, CodeQL, secret scanning, user push protection, dependency review, private vulnerability reporting and free Actions minutes, all at no cost.
(b) Private repo on Pro. You get rulesets or branch protection, required status checks, CODEOWNERS and environments, but no CodeQL, secret scanning, dependency review or private vulnerability reporting.
(c) Private repo on Free. There is no server-side enforcement at all, so everything below rests on local hooks plus CI that you promise not to bypass.
I recommend (a) if you are willing to open-source a local-first tool, otherwise (b).

Ruleset on `main` for a solo developer:
- require a pull request with 0 approvals, because authors cannot approve their own PRs;
- require status checks, pointing at a single aggregate job such as `ci-ok`;
- require linear history;
- block force pushes;
- restrict deletions;
- keep yourself on the bypass list only for emergencies.
You can run anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 as an advisory reviewer. It cannot count as the required approval.

LOCAL ENFORCEMENT
Use lefthook (lefthook.yml; installs through npm or pnpm, winget or scoop; supports parallel jobs, `{staged_files}` globs and `stage_fixed`; https://lefthook.dev/). npm latest is 2.1.14. I prefer it to husky (npm latest 9.1.7, last published 2024-11) because it is language-agnostic, which covers the Python-alternative case, and runs jobs in parallel.
- pre-commit: gitleaks on staged changes, then the formatter and linter on staged files, then tsc --noEmit.
- commit-msg: commitlint with @commitlint/config-conventional (npm @commitlint/cli 21.2.3).
- pre-push: the branch-name regex, refusing a direct push to main, and `vitest run`.
If you choose the Python stack, the pre-commit framework is equivalent: install the commit-msg stage with `pre-commit install --hook-type commit-msg`, and run `pre-commit run --all-files` in CI (https://pre-commit.com/).
Hooks can be skipped with --no-verify, so CI must re-run every hook check. On private Free repos, CI plus your own discipline is the only backstop.

testingTools.purpose: Fast unit tests for parsing captured thoughts, linking them to a person and a conversation, rendering briefs, and the data-access layer. Includes built-in benchmarking through Tinybench, and experimental type tests with expectTypeOf.

Properties such as: export then import returns identical data; every note linked to a conversation appears in its brief; renaming a person never orphans notes; markdown and JSON escaping never breaks structure.
Drive the note store with random sequences of create, link, archive, delete, restore and migrate against a simple in-memory model, to catch ordering bugs in delete, undo and archive logic.
The same property and stateful coverage if you take the Python 3.13 / uv route (PyPI: hypothesis 6.168.1, pytest 9.1.1).

Measures whether tests actually catch bugs in core logic (brief assembly, privacy filters, delete paths). Supports incremental mode; run it nightly or on labelled PRs. Limitations: no Vitest browser mode, and coverage analysis is always per-test.
Mutation testing for pytest suites. Needs fork() support, so on Windows it must run inside WSL, or run it in Linux CI only.

The docs note that InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair only connects 2025-era instances, so use handler.fetch for 2026-07-28 coverage. Test stdio by spawning the process with StdioClientTransport.

testingTools.purpose: The same in-process client/server tests for a Python server (PyPI: mcp 2.2.0, fastmcp 4.0.10).

A connect, list, call, assert smoke test on every commit and deploy: `npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@<exact> --cli node dist/server.js -- --method tools/list`, with `--format json` plus jq, stable exit codes and `--connect-timeout`. Pin an exact version in CI. Needs Node >= 22.19.

testingTools.purpose: If a tool declares outputSchema, the server MUST return conforming structuredContent. Servers SHOULD return tools in a deterministic order. Snapshot tool names, descriptions and schemas so any contract change is deliberate, reviewed and semver-bumped. Descriptions are also an injection surface.

Cases live in evals/<case>/ as prompt.md plus graders (regex, tool_used, llm), with mocked MCP tools. Each case runs 3 times with the plugin and 3 without, as a no-plugin baseline. In CI use `--threshold 0.8 --model <pinned> --judge-model <pinned> --trust-plugin --no-publish --max-cost-usd 20`, and gate on the exit code. Include 'must not trigger' cases and a Skill tool_used grader.

testingTools.purpose: Iterating on SKILL.md while you write it: benchmark pass rate, time and tokens (mean and standard deviation) against a baseline, and optimise the description's triggering with should_trigger / should_not_trigger queries through `claude -p`. Its case format is separate from `claude plugin eval`.
