threatConsiderations.risk: Stored (indirect) prompt injection through note content: OWASP LLM01 and MCP06
threatConsiderations.description: RTO stores free text from you and from others: pasted emails, Pocket transcripts, calendar event descriptions. It later returns that text to Claude in tool results. Instructions hidden in a note can steer Claude, and your session also has Gmail, Calendar and Trello connectors that can send data out. That combination is Willison's 'lethal trifecta': private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel. OWASP 2026 v1.0 (published 2026-08) keeps prompt injection at #1.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Treat every note as data. Return notes only inside structuredContent fields, never in tool descriptions or prompts. RTO itself should expose no outbound or 'send' tools. Keep read tools read-only and ask for confirmation on anything destructive. Apply context minimization: return only the notes for the selected person and conversation. Consider the plan-then-execute or dual-LLM patterns for any automation. Label imported text by source ('from: transcript'). Run promptfoo indirect-prompt-injection tests on poisoned fixtures in CI.

threatConsiderations.risk: Sensitive information disclosure (LLM02) about third parties
threatConsiderations.description: Notes about a spouse, manager or client are sensitive. They can leak through over-broad retrieval into unrelated chats, through briefs shared with the wrong person, through logs, or through model-provider retention. On consumer Claude plans, opting in to training means 5-year retention; opting out keeps 30 days. Commercial and API terms are excluded from that change.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Scope every read tool by person or conversation ID and paginate. Add a 'private / never send to model' flag that the server enforces. Document the data flow to Anthropic in the README. Use API or commercial terms for any hosted multi-user version. Never log note bodies.

threatConsiderations.risk: Excessive agency (LLM06:2025, LLM03 in 2026) and destructive tools
threatConsiderations.description: Tools such as delete_person, purge or sync could be triggered by a confused or injected model. Clients MUST treat tool annotations such as destructiveHint as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Expose a minimal tool set. Use soft-delete with an undo window, and require explicit confirmation for hard delete (in the 2026-07-28 spec, through an input-required result or elicitation). Validate all inputs on the server, rate-limit tool calls, and sanitize outputs, as the tools spec requires.

threatConsiderations.risk: Token passthrough and confused deputy (remote phase, especially if RTO proxies Google Calendar or Gmail)
threatConsiderations.description: A server that accepts tokens not issued to it, or forwards client tokens downstream, breaks audience boundaries. An MCP proxy that uses a static third-party client ID together with dynamic client registration can let an attacker skip consent and steal authorization codes.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: MCP servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them. Validate audience per RFC 8707 and send the resource parameter. If RTO proxies third-party APIs: record consent per client_id, use exact redirect_uri matching, and single-use state that expires within about 10 minutes. Consent cookies use the __Host- prefix and Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax. Prevent framing with frame-ancestors.

threatConsiderations.risk: OAuth implementation errors in the remote MCP server
threatConsiderations.description: The 2026-07-28 spec requires OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), resource indicators (RFC 8707) and issuer validation (RFC 9207). It prefers Client ID Metadata Documents and deprecates Dynamic Client Registration. Refresh tokens MUST be kept confidential in storage. CIMD also introduces SSRF and localhost-redirect impersonation risks on the authorization server.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Do not write your own authorization server: use a hosted identity provider that supports CIMD, PKCE and iss. Set scopes_supported to a minimal set and step up with scope challenges. Run the conformance auth scenarios. Store refresh tokens encrypted.

threatConsiderations.risk: State handle hijacking / IDOR (replaces 'session hijacking' in 2026-07-28; session IDs still matter for 2025-11-25 clients)
threatConsiderations.description: The protocol is now stateless. Note, person and brief IDs passed as tool arguments act as handles; if possessing one is treated as authorization, another user can read or modify that data.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Never treat possession of a handle as authentication. Key stored data by <user_id from the verified token>:<handle>. Use random, non-sequential IDs (UUIDv4 or ULID) with expiry where suitable. Add BOLA/BFLA tests with promptfoo plugins and ZAP.

threatConsiderations.risk: Local server exposure: DNS rebinding and local-process abuse
threatConsiderations.description: A local HTTP MCP server bound to 0.0.0.0, or without Origin validation, can be driven by malicious websites through DNS rebinding, or by other local processes.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Use stdio for the local MVP. If you use HTTP: validate the Origin header and return 403 when it is invalid, bind to 127.0.0.1, and require an auth token. Never run shell commands built from note text.

threatConsiderations.description: MCP clients, and authorization servers that fetch CIMD URLs, can be steered to internal addresses (169.254.169.254, localhost services). This also applies if RTO ever fetches URLs found in notes.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Do not fetch URLs on the server in the MVP. If you add it later: require HTTPS, block private and link-local ranges with a vetted library (not hand-rolled parsing), validate every redirect hop, and route egress through a proxy such as Smokescreen.

threatConsiderations.description: Recent incidents: the self-replicating Shai-Hulud worm compromised more than 500 npm packages (CISA alert, 2025-09-23), and trivy-action tags were hijacked (2026-03-19). Both stole CI and developer credentials.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Set pnpm minimumReleaseAge (days, not minutes), strictDepBuilds with allowBuilds, and trustPolicy no-downgrade. Install with a frozen lockfile. Pin actions by SHA, enforced by repo policy. Set a least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN and run zizmor. Use a Dependabot cooldown. Protect GitHub and npm accounts with phishing-resistant MFA. Attach an SBOM to each release. Keep dependencies few.

threatConsiderations.description: Hard-coded or long-lived credentials (the Anthropic API key in CI, OAuth refresh tokens, the database encryption key) end up in repos, logs or model context.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Keep secrets in the OS keychain (@napi-rs/keyring) and GitHub Actions secrets; prefer OIDC or workload identity federation where supported. Run gitleaks in pre-commit and in CI, never echo secrets, and redact them in error messages.

threatConsiderations.risk: Tool poisoning and shadow MCP servers (MCP03, MCP09)
threatConsiderations.description: Other MCP servers in the same client can carry malicious tool descriptions that tell Claude to call RTO's read tools and exfiltrate the results. Claude Code loads project .mcp.json servers without a prompt in -p mode.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Keep RTO tool descriptions static, short and snapshot-tested. Document that users should enable only trusted servers alongside RTO. In CI, use `claude --bare` and never run Claude on untrusted fork PRs with secrets.

threatConsiderations.risk: Lack of audit and telemetry (MCP08) versus privacy
threatConsiderations.description: You need to know which tool ran and when, for incident response, without logging private content.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Keep content-free structured audit logs: tool name, IDs, counts, result status, correlation ID. Follow the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet exclusions (tokens, PII, keys). Log to stderr for stdio (MCP Logging is deprecated in 2026-07-28), or to OpenTelemetry with payload capture off.

threatConsiderations.description: Large note histories can overflow context or cost; Claude Code's default MCP output limit is 25,000 tokens.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: Paginate, cap results, and summarise on the server where deterministic. Rate-limit calls. Add benchmarks and k6 thresholds for the remote endpoint.

threatConsiderations.risk: CI workflow injection (pull_request_target, template injection, over-privileged tokens)
threatConsiderations.description: Workflows that interpolate untrusted PR titles or bodies, or grant write tokens, can be hijacked. A compromised action gets every secret in the job.
threatConsiderations.mitigation: zizmor in CI; `permissions: {}` at workflow level with explicit per-job grants; no pull_request_target on untrusted code; pinned SHAs; environments for deploy secrets (private environments need Pro).

privacyPractices: Local-first by default: the MVP stores everything on the user's machine and talks to Claude through a stdio MCP server, with no cloud component. This follows the Ink & Switch local-first ideals, including 'security and privacy by default' and 'you retain ultimate ownership' (https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/).

Encrypt at rest with SQLite3 Multiple Ciphers, through better-sqlite3-multiple-ciphers (npm 13.0.3). Its default is sqleet ChaCha20-Poly1305, which authenticates data and so detects tampering. A SQLCipher-compatible AES-256 + HMAC mode is also available (https://utelle.github.io/SQLite3MultipleCiphers/ ; https://github.com/m4heshd/better-sqlite3-multiple-ciphers). For Python, use SQLCipher through sqlcipher3 (https://www.zetetic.net/sqlcipher/). Avoid the legacy AES-CBC and RC4 modes, which have no HMAC.

Key management: generate a random 256-bit key and store it in the OS credential store with @napi-rs/keyring (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service; MIT; npm 2.1.0). Do not use keytar, which was archived on 2022-12-15 (https://github.com/Brooooooklyn/keyring-node ; https://github.com/atom/node-keytar). Never put the key in .env, config files or logs. Support rekey for rotation, and offer an optional recovery passphrase for backups.

Data minimisation (GDPR Art. 25: 'data protection by design and by default'). Store only what a brief needs: a person alias and relationship label, not contact details. Do not keep raw audio or full transcripts from Pocket; keep the extracted points. Add per-note retention, for example archiving after the conversation happens and purging after N days unless the note is pinned (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-25-gdpr/).

Control what reaches the model. Every brief Claude generates sends note text to Anthropic. On consumer plans, opting in to training means 5-year retention versus 30 days if you opt out; commercial and API terms are excluded (https://www.anthropic.com/news/updates-to-our-consumer-terms). Provide a server-enforced 'never send to model' flag and a sensitive-category warning, and state the data flow plainly in the README.

Export: a one-command, human-readable export (Markdown plus JSON with a schema version) and matching import, covered by round-trip property tests. This gives users portability now and supports GDPR Art. 20 duties if RTO becomes multi-user.

Delete: offer per-note, per-person and whole-store deletion. Use soft-delete with an undo window, then hard delete plus VACUUM so freed pages do not linger. Backups follow a stated retention window so deletions age out of them. Test delete with the model-based fast-check suite. Always encrypt backups (better-sqlite3 .backup() on the encrypted handle) and restore-test them in CI (https://github.com/WiseLibs/better-sqlite3/blob/master/docs/api.md).

Log hygiene: never log note bodies, names, tokens, keys or connection strings. Remove, mask or pseudonymise sensitive data, and strip CR/LF to prevent log injection, per the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html). For stdio servers, log to stderr only; MCP's Logging feature is deprecated in spec 2026-07-28 (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog). No telemetry by default; any opt-in telemetry is content-free.

Threat-model privacy explicitly with LINDDUN (Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance) alongside STRIDE, in OWASP Threat Dragon, and repeat it at each phase change: local, then remote, then multi-user (https://linddun.org/ ; https://owasp.org/www-project-threat-dragon/).

GDPR if RTO becomes a multi-user service. Recital 18 exempts an individual keeping notes for purely personal or household purposes, but it states the Regulation still applies to controllers or processors that provide the means for such processing. As the provider you would therefore be in scope (https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-18/). GDPR has no revenue threshold, unlike the CCPA.

GDPR and third parties: the people written about are data subjects whose data was not obtained from them. Art. 14 requires telling them unless that proves impossible or disproportionate (Art. 14(5)(b)), and even then safeguards are needed (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-14-gdpr/). My inference, not legal advice: a hosted RTO should be positioned as a processor for users' household use where possible, and should prohibit special-category data (health, politics, sexuality) in its terms and UI. It will probably need a DPIA, Art. 32 security measures and a sub-processor agreement with the model provider. Confirm with counsel before launch.

CCPA/CPRA applies only to for-profit businesses that meet one threshold: $26.625M gross annual revenue (effective 2025-01-01), buying, selling or sharing personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households, or earning 50% or more of revenue from selling or sharing personal information (https://cppa.ca.gov/faq.html). A solo MVP is very likely below all three. The CPPA adopted regulations on risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decision-making technology in September 2025 (https://cppa.ca.gov/regulations/). I did not verify other US state privacy laws.

Remote and multi-user phase design: prefer end-to-end or client-side encryption so the server holds only ciphertext, where features allow (the local-first ideal). If server-side processing is required, use per-user keys, row-level isolation, handles bound to the verified user ID, region choice, and a documented breach-response runbook.

Secrets and tokens for integrations such as Google Calendar and Gmail: request the narrowest OAuth scopes. The MCP spec requires refresh tokens to be kept confidential in storage. Keep them in the keychain, never in the notes database or in logs (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/authorization).

checkedClaims.correction: None. The docs' 'Who can use this feature?' box says protected branches are available in public repositories on GitHub Free, and in public and private repositories on Pro, Team, Enterprise Cloud and Server. The admin-bypass default is stated as described.

checkedClaims.claim: Branch/tag rulesets are available on Free public repos and on Pro private repos but not on Free private repos. They allow up to 75 per repo, anyone with read access can view them, and the enforcement statuses listed are only Active and Disabled (no Evaluate).
checkedClaims.correction: None. The page says 'Rulesets are available in public repositories with GitHub Free... and in public and private repositories with GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud', and lists only the Active and Disabled statuses. Commit-metadata rules are documented only in the Enterprise Cloud docs.

checkedClaims.claim: Push rulesets are available only on GitHub Team, for private and internal repos, so a Pro user cannot use them.
checkedClaims.correction: None. The docs say 'Push rulesets are available for the GitHub Team plan in internal and private repositories, and forks of repositories that have push rulesets enabled.'

checkedClaims.claim: Pull request authors cannot approve their own PRs, so a solo developer must set required approvals to 0 or rely on bypass. Required status checks default to 'strict' (branch must be up to date).
checkedClaims.correction: None. The docs state 'Pull request authors cannot approve their own pull requests.' The rules page says strict is 'the default behavior for required status checks'.

checkedClaims.correction: None. Code scanning is available for 'Public repositories on GitHub.com' and for 'Organization-owned repositories on GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, or GitHub Enterprise Server, with GitHub Code Security enabled'. The CodeQL licence bars use 'in connection with any codebase that is not an Open Source Codebase (e.g., code in a private repo in GitHub)' unless you have a paid GHAS licence. The GHAS page says Code Security and Secret Protection 'are available for accounts on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud'.

checkedClaims.correction: None. For user-owned repositories the docs list only Enterprise Cloud with Enterprise Managed Users, or Enterprise Server with Secret Protection.

checkedClaims.claim: On free public repos only user-level push protection is on by default; repository-level push protection needs GitHub Secret Protection.
checkedClaims.correction: GitHub's changelog says 'All new public repositories owned by personal accounts will now have secret scanning and push protection enabled by default', and push protection is free for all public repos. On a public personal repo, repository-level push protection is therefore free and on by default for new repos. The current docs line 'Requires GitHub Secret Protection' effectively applies to private and internal repos. The changelog is from 2024-03, so it may be stale; check the repo's Security settings after creating it.

checkedClaims.correction: None. Dependency review is available for 'Public repositories on GitHub.com' and 'Organization-owned repositories on GitHub Team with GitHub Code Security enabled'. checkedClaims.correction: None. checkedClaims.claim: MCP spec 2026-07-28 is current. It makes the protocol stateless (no sessions or initialize), deprecates Dynamic Client Registration in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents, deprecates Logging (log to stderr or OpenTelemetry), adds ttlMs caching and input_required (MRTR) results, and says servers SHOULD return tools in a deterministic order.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed; /specification/latest redirects to 2026-07-28. However, Claude's own connector client is documented as following only the 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25 authorization specs, and as not supporting 'advanced or draft capabilities', sampling or resource subscriptions. Designs that depend on 2026-07-28-only behaviour (MRTR input_required confirmations for hard delete, ttlMs) may not work in Claude clients yet. See omissions.

checkedClaims.claim: MCP TypeScript SDK v2: @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client are at 2.1.0. Testing uses createMcpHandler with handler.fetch and a real Client. InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair connects only 2025-era instances.
checkedClaims.correction: None. Both packages are at 2.1.0 on npm (2026-09-23). The testing doc says '`createLinkedPair` connects 2025-era instances only; `handler.fetch` is the in-process entry for 2026-07-28 coverage.' v1 (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.1) will get fixes 'for at least 6 months after v2's release'.

checkedClaims.correction: npm 'latest' is indeed 0.1.16, but it predates the 2026-07-28 spec. The TS SDK's conformance package pins '@modelcontextprotocol/conformance': '0.2.0-alpha.11' (npm alpha tag, 2026-08-07) and runs '--spec-version 2026-07-28' with a separate expected-failures.2026-07-28.yaml. Pin 0.2.0-alpha.11 (or the SDK's current pin) for 2026-07-28 scenarios; 0.1.16 covers only older specs.

checkedClaims.claim: `claude plugin eval` exists. Cases live in evals/<case>/prompt.md with regex, tool_used and llm graders and mocked MCP tools, and each case runs 3 times with the plugin and 3 without. CI flags: --threshold, --model, --judge-model, --trust-plugin, --no-publish, --max-cost-usd, gating on the exit code.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed. Additional details: the default --threshold is 1.0. Grader types are regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists, llm and baseline. Exit code 2 means a partial run (cost ceiling hit). When signed in with a claude.ai subscription, the HTML report is published as a private artifact by default unless you pass --no-publish, which matters if fixtures contain real notes.

checkedClaims.claim: `claude --bare -p` skips hooks, .mcp.json and CLAUDE.md, needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and supports --json-schema with structured_output. system/init reports plugin_errors and mcp_server_errors. Without --bare, -p loads project .mcp.json servers without prompting. Claude Code's default MCP output limit is 25,000 tokens.

checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed as announced on 2025-08-28. It covers Free, Pro and Max, including Claude Code on those accounts, and excludes Claude for Work, Government, Education and the API (including Bedrock and Vertex). The source is about 13 months old, so re-check the current policy.

checkedClaims.claim: The CCPA/CPRA revenue threshold is $26.625M (effective 2025-01-01). The other thresholds are 100,000 or more CA consumers or households, or 50% or more of revenue from selling or sharing personal information.
checkedClaims.correction: None. The threshold is CPI-adjusted in odd years, so expect a change around 2027-01-01.

checkedClaims.claim: OpenAI announced its acquisition of promptfoo on 2026-03-09, and promptfoo remains open source. OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 v1.0 was published in 2026-08 with prompt injection still #1 and excessive agency now #3.
checkedClaims.correction: None. The promptfoo post (2026-03-09) says it 'will remain open source' and will support 'a diverse range of providers'; it does not name Anthropic or restate the MIT licence (npm shows MIT for 0.123.1). The OWASP resource page shows v1.0, published 2026-08-03. ReversingLabs (2026-08-12) reports excessive agency moved from 6th to 3rd.

checkedClaims.claim: CISA's 2025-09-23 alert says the Shai-Hulud worm compromised more than 500 npm packages. keytar was archived on 2022-12-15. nvie's 'Note of reflection' is dated 2020-03-05 and recommends GitHub Flow for continuous delivery.
checkedClaims.correction: None. All three were verified against the primary pages; the GitHub page shows keytar 'archived by the owner on Dec 15, 2022'.

checkedClaims.claim: SQLite3 Multiple Ciphers defaults to sqleet ChaCha20-Poly1305 (authenticated). The legacy wxSQLite3 AES-CBC and RC4 modes lack HMAC. mutmut needs fork(), so it must run in WSL on Windows.
checkedClaims.correction: None. SQLite3MC also offers Ascon-128 and AEGIS schemes. mutmut docs: 'if you want to run on windows, you must run inside WSL.'

checkedClaims.claim: GDPR Recital 18 exempts purely personal or household processing, but the Regulation still applies to controllers or processors that provide the means for such processing.
checkedClaims.correction: Confirmed verbatim. The exemption covers only activity 'with no connection to a professional or commercial activity'. RTO's core use cases (manager, client, contractor) are professional, so even the user's own notes may fall outside it (my inference, not legal advice).

omissions: Claude does not yet support MCP 2026-07-28. Claude's connector docs say its OAuth client follows the 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25 authorization specs, and that it does not support resource subscriptions, sampling or 'advanced or draft capabilities'. The research builds around 2026-07-28 features: stateless handles, MRTR input_required confirmation for hard delete, ttlMs and Logging deprecation. The server must also serve 2025-11-25-style clients (initialize and sessions), and tests should cover both. Do not rely on MRTR or elicitation for delete confirmation in claude.ai without testing it. Source: https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/index

Hosted Claude surfaces have their own limits: about 150,000 characters maximum tool result and a 240 s tool-call timeout on claude.ai and Desktop. The research cites only Claude Code's 25k-token limit. The OAuth redirect URI to allow is https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback, plus a loopback redirect for Claude Code. Source: https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/index

Custom connectors are called from Anthropic's cloud, so the server 'must be reachable over the public internet from Anthropic's IP ranges'. The research's local-first stdio MVP therefore cannot be used from claude.ai web or the mobile apps. That conflicts with the core 'capture on the go' job, and mobile capture needs a remote server (with the full OAuth and security scope) or a separate capture path. Free plans are limited to one custom connector. Source: https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp

MCP tunnels, which reach a private-network server without a public endpoint, are an Enterprise-only research preview. They are not a route for a solo developer. Source: https://claude.com/docs/connectors/mcp-tunnels/overview

Desktop extensions (MCPB .mcpb bundles) are the documented way to package and install a local MCP server in Claude Desktop without editing config by hand. This is a natural phase-1 distribution step that the research does not mention. Claude's add-connector UI recommends 'Use Claude's published identity' (an Anthropic-hosted CIMD) and still supports DCR. Source: https://claude.com/docs/connectors/custom/remote-mcp

GitHub announced a $0.002/min platform charge for self-hosted runners on private repos (originally due 2026-03-01). It is postponed but 'under evaluation', so 'self-hosted runners are free' may change. Source: https://github.com/resources/insights/2026-pricing-changes-for-github-actions

GitHub's docs conflict on Pro storage: the plans page lists 2 GB of GitHub Packages storage for Pro, while the Actions billing page lists 1 GB of shared artifact and Packages storage. Copilot code review also consumes Actions minutes on private repos. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans
The Trivy advisory also covers aquasecurity/setup-trivy before 0.2.6, which the research omitted.

Version freshness conflicts with the research's own supply-chain advice. Vitest 5.0.0 shipped 2026-09-03 and 5.0.2 on 2026-09-25 (today). The research recommends pnpm minimumReleaseAge of 3 to 7 days (default 1 day) together with pinning the newest versions, and those two will clash on install. @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner 10.0.0 declares vitest >=2.0.0 but does not document Vitest 5 support, so test it before relying on mutation testing.

claude plugin eval publishes its HTML report as a private claude.ai artifact by default when signed in with a subscription. Local eval runs on fixtures derived from real notes should pass --no-publish, not just CI runs.
The research does not verify an official GitHub Pro price. The pricing page omits Pro, and third-party sites claim $4/month (unverified).
verification.summary:
I checked 27 claims; 25 held up on primary sources and 2 were refuted. Most GitHub plan facts (rulesets and protected branches, and which scanning features are public-repo-only) match GitHub's own docs, as do the Actions quotas and rates, pnpm and Dependabot details, the CodeQL licence, gitleaks, Harden-Runner, Scorecard, the Trivy incident, the MCP 2026-07-28 changelog, TS SDK v2 testing, `claude plugin eval`, headless `--bare`, Anthropic retention terms, the CCPA threshold, promptfoo/OpenAI and the OWASP 2026 list.

Refuted:
1. **Public-repo push protection:** new public repos owned by personal accounts get secret scanning and push protection on by default for free (GitHub changelog, March 2024, possibly stale). It does not need Secret Protection on public repos.
2. **Conformance version:** npm latest 0.1.16 predates the 2026-07-28 spec. The TS SDK pins 0.2.0-alpha.11 with `--spec-version 2026-07-28`.

Most decision-relevant omissions:
- **MCP version gap:** Claude's connector client is documented against the 2025-era auth specs (up to 2025-11-25) and does not support draft or advanced capabilities. Features that exist only in 2026-07-28 (stateless handles, input_required confirmations) may not work in Claude yet.
- **Connectors need a public server:** custom connectors are called from Anthropic's cloud and need a publicly reachable server. A local-first stdio MVP therefore cannot support mobile or web capture on the go.
- **No tunnel route for a solo developer:** MCP tunnels are Enterprise-only.
- **Local packaging route:** MCPB desktop extensions are the documented way to install a local server in Claude Desktop.
- **Self-hosted runner fee:** a $0.002/min self-hosted runner charge was postponed, not cancelled.

Web search and fetch worked, but Firecrawl was out of credits, so I pulled GitHub docs through curl.
